To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a normal ECG in a patient who has chest pain and is at low risk for a myocardial infarct or unstable angina does not rule out these disorders.

a normal ECG is a good indicator of a very-low-risk patient, but that no single variable can accurately identify low-risk patients and that a combination of variables, which we call the chest pain index, can be used to identify a low-risk patient.

a combination of three variables from the history and physical examination can identify patients at very low risk for myocardium infarction, that the ECG is of little help in this situation, that the combination of history, physical examination, and ECG can identify patients at moderate risk for myocardial ischemia, and that the ECG alone can identify patients at high risk for myocardial damage.

the development of a system that can be used in a clinical environment to help the clinician to identify the patient at low risk for acute myocardial infarct.
the identification of low-risk patients who come to an emergency room with chest pain.

the ECG is a useful adjunct in the emergency room evaluation of acute chest pain, and it should be obtained in all patients.

the ECG, when normal in patients who present with acute chest pain, is a very strong indicator that myocardial infarctions and unstable anginas are very unlikely to be occurring, but it is not a conclusive indicator.
the ECG is an essential part of the initial evaluation in patients who present to the emergency room with chest pain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the emergency room evaluation of chest pain is a very complex process, and that the ECG is an essential part of the process, but that it is not the only important component.
a normal ECG does not identify low-risk patients with chest pain.
in the absence of a normal electrocardiogram, the absence of chest pain that is pleuritic or sharp or that is reproduced by palpation is a strong indicator of a cardiac event.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the emergency room is a place for clinical judgment.
the ECG is a very important part of the evaluation of patients with chest pain in the ED.
the ECG is a critical tool in the emergency room evaluation of chest pain, but it should be considered in combination with the history and physical examination, not as a stand-alone test.
